methodological_rigor.justification: This retrospective reader study includes 45,602 women from two NHSBSP centers with 39-month follow-up and a pre-specified primary endpoint of noninferiority (5% margin) using Wald test and Obuchowski variance estimation for clustered data. A 22-reader arbitration panel with structured training (including 100 training cases) and carefully transcribed anonymized paperwork strengthens internal validity. Key strengths include longitudinal outcome data enabling sensitivity analysis by time of cancer detection, localization analysis, and human factors assessment. The 8.7% AI exclusion rate and inability to blind readers to the AI arm (AI output overlaid on images) are acknowledged limitations. The finding that arbitration reverses early detection gains for interval/next-round cancers is a nuanced and important methodological observation.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Large retrospective cohort study (Oxford LoE 2b) directly addressing a critical operational gap: the impact of AI second-reader replacement on arbitration outcomes in double-read breast screening. The demonstration that arbitration can reverse AI's early detection advantage for interval and next-round cancers (AI sensitivity before arbitration 32.4% vs after 8.8% for interval cancers) is clinically important for NHS screening program planning. The workload analysis showing 36-44% reading time reduction adds direct health system relevance.

reporting_quality.justification: The study follows STARD reporting for diagnostic accuracy, with a Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary referenced. The case selection, data curation, exclusion criteria, reader training, arbitration protocol, statistical analysis plan, and localization ground truth methodology are all described in sufficient detail. Subgroup analyses are pre-specified and clearly labeled as exploratory without multiple comparison correction. The human factors surveys are transparently reported. The OPTIMAM database provides a recognized infrastructure for data access.

novelty_literature.justification: This study uniquely incorporates a prospective reader study for the arbitration component, distinguishing it from prior retrospective simulations of AI-in-double-reading workflows. The key novel finding—that arbitration substantially reduces AI's pre-arbitration advantage for interval and next-round cancers, raising questions about whether arbitration panels trained on human-only workflows are optimal for AI-assisted review—has direct policy implications for NHS screening program implementation and is not previously documented in the literature.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well organized and methodologically transparent, with clear presentation of sensitivity by time of cancer detection and detailed arbitration outcome analysis. Tables 2-4 provide comprehensive performance metrics with appropriate confidence intervals. The discussion clearly contextualizes the seven key aspects of the results and their implementation implications. The human factors analysis adds a valuable practical dimension. The complexity of the dual-center, dual-arm design is managed clearly through consistent notation and figures.

key_strengths: Novel incorporation of a prospective reader study (22 radiologists) for the arbitration component, enabling realistic rather than simulated assessment of AI impact on double-read breast screening with arbitration
Longitudinal 39-month ground truth enabling sensitivity analysis by cancer detection time, revealing that arbitration reverses AI's pre-arbitration advantage for interval and next-round cancers
Noninferior sensitivity and specificity for AI arm vs human arm post-arbitration (P<0.001), with 40% overall reading time reduction
Transparent human factors analysis revealing reader dissatisfaction patterns and the role of prior imaging in arbitration overruling decisions
key_concerns: Inability to blind readers to the AI arm (AI output overlaid on images) introduces potential bias in arbitration decisions, though acknowledged as clinically realistic
Study limited to two London NHS centers using one AI system (Google v1.2) and one operating point per center, limiting generalizability

Finding that arbitration eliminates AI's early detection benefit for interval cancers raises important clinical concern that is not fully resolved by the current study design—no proposed solution for adapting arbitration training for AI-assisted workflows
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a methodologically rigorous and clinically important study that uniquely captures the impact of AI on the full double-read arbitration workflow, with the finding about arbitration reversing early detection gains representing a novel and actionable insight for breast screening program planning at Tier 2.
